claim: Conditionalization is the rule Cr'(X)=Cr(X and E)/Cr(E): evidence-incompatible possibilities go to zero and survivors keep their ratios; it is undefined when Cr(E)=0. (Definition; only SEP opened. Ramsey, de Finetti, Bayes originals not read.)
agent_test: Unit test: code normaliser over exclusive answers after eliminating options; check ratios among survivors are unchanged.

claim: Conditionalization has known limits: uncertain evidence (needs Jeffrey), old evidence, new theories, memory loss, and prior dependence. It does not say how to choose priors or likelihoods.
agent_test: Log cases where the agent meets a new hypothesis mid-run; check it re-seeds the option set instead of renormalising over a stale set.

claim: A diachronic Dutch-book argument supports conditionalization (sure loss = [Pr1(A|E)-Pr2(A)] x Pr1(E)); Skyrms proved a converse. Critics dispute that it shows a rational requirement.
agent_test: Not directly testable; use as design rationale only.

claim: Humans update too little from sample evidence (conservatism/underinference): pooled slope of subjective on Bayes log-odds is 0.20; 8:4 draws give about .70 vs Bayes .97. The effect depends on sample size (mean slope 0.52-1.06 for samples of 2-6).
agent_test: Compare LLM stated posterior vs computed Bayes posterior on bookbag items of growing sample size, at equal tokens.
audit_note: The 0.20 pooled slope is specifically for the N=1-sample studies (Figure 2 Panel A), and per-N slopes at 3 and 5 are not below 1 (0.98, 1.06), so the 0.52-1.06 range includes no-underinference cases. 8:4 .7 vs .97 is Edwards via Wikipedia (secondary); 0.231/(0.231+0.008)=0.967 checks.

claim: People under-use base rates: in the Kahneman-Tversky engineer-lawyer task (30 vs 70 percent engineers) mean judgments were about 50 vs 55 percent, an odds ratio of about 1.2 against the Bayesian 5.4, which is near-complete neglect (complete for an uninformative description); some other experiments find partial use of base rates (Koehler 1996, via Benjamin 2019).
agent_test: Run base-rate items with prior stated in prompt vs computed in code; measure prior weight.
audit_note: Benjamin 2019 says Kahneman-Tversky found complete base-rate neglect in some experiments and only partial neglect in others (Koehler 1996); the cited engineer-lawyer example (ratio 1.2 vs Bayes 5.4; Dick case 50% in both groups) is near-complete neglect, so 'usually partially' is not supported by the example. Numbers 5.4 and 1.2 match; Benjamin's text labels the groups the other way round (55% for the 30-engineer group). Wikipedia gives no figures.
claim_before_audit: People under-use base rates but usually partially, not completely (engineer-lawyer 30 vs 70 percent gave 50 vs 55 percent; Bayes odds ratio 5.4 vs about 1.2).

claim: Natural-frequency formats raise Bayesian accuracy, but the size and mechanism are contested. Primary paper (Gigerenzer and Hoffrage 1995, Study 1, N=60, strict process-plus-outcome criterion): probability format 16% (standard menu) and 28% (short menu), frequency format 46% and 50%. The 22 vs 48 figure is the menu average, so 16/46 and 22/48 are both right. Study 2 (N=15): 6.4% and 17.5% in probability formats. 2025 replication: 36.2 vs 21.6 percent for one test and reversed for two sequential tests (4.9 vs 10.6). In LLMs (2023 models) a facilitated natural-count HIV problem was answered correctly more often by all models except Llama 2.
agent_test: Restate probability problems as counts out of N before computing; compare accuracy with a plain-probability prompt on 2025-26 models (not yet tested).

claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not update like a Bayesian across rounds: accuracy stalls after round 1 in a 5-round preference task; CoT, numeric encodings and 30 rounds did not fix it.
agent_test: Replicate a small multi-round elimination task with and without code-side posterior; same token budget.

claim: Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's guesses beats fine-tuning on an oracle's answers and generalises to new domains (agreement with Bayesian assistant about 80 percent).
agent_test: Out of scope for a scaffold. Use only as evidence that the gap is about update behaviour, not knowledge.

claim: LLMs without tools violate the martingale property and Bayes coherence; violations are common across separate conversations (over 50 percent) and smaller within one dialogue.
agent_test: Ask for P(A), P(not A) and P(A or B) in separate calls; count normalisation and monotonicity breaks with and without a code normaliser.
audit_note: Over-50% figure is violation rate over 30 Dutch-book scenarios in Filbry et al. (cross-conversation), dropping markedly within one dialogue; Falck shows martingale violations; stronger/tool-equipped models do better, consistent with 'without tools'.

claim: CORRECTED. One-evidence-at-a-time updating with the model's own stated likelihood is closer to Bayes (more internally consistent) than batch updating, and GPT-5.1 was near-optimal in that mode. But batch updating gave equal or better task performance (AUROC, ECE) on 3 of 4 datasets, and forcing an explicit Bayes posterior from the model's own likelihoods did not reliably help and hurt on MediQ. Separately, an externally computed oracle posterior is followed far better with reasoning, and with code execution when the posterior has no closed form (small-N, mostly 26-35B models).
agent_test: Compare batch posterior, per-evidence code posterior and code posterior with oracle-quality likelihoods at equal tokens, scoring accuracy not consistency. Do not assume per-evidence updating raises accuracy.

claim: In one preprint (Zhang et al. 2025, discounted Bayesian filters) in-context belief updates in changing environments were better described by an exponential forgetting filter with gamma below 1 than by exact Bayes, whereas Gupta et al. 2025 (static coin flips) found updates broadly Bayesian with deviations mainly from miscalibrated priors, and non-instruct models failed to converge to a priors stated explicitly in the prompt.
agent_test: Insert a stated prior in the prompt and measure whether the answer shifts as Bayes predicts.
audit_note: Only Zhang et al. (arXiv 2512.18489, a single short preprint) finds a discounted filter (gamma below 1, e.g. 0.88 for Llama-3.1-8B) fits better than exact Bayes; Gupta et al. conclude LLMs broadly follow Bayesian posterior updates, with deviations mainly from miscalibrated priors, so the sources point in partly different directions. Gupta supports wrong priors and non-instruct models failing to converge to an explicit stated bias.
claim_before_audit: LLM in-context updating is better fit by a discounted filter (gamma below 1) than by exact Bayes, and priors from pretraining are wrong and slow to correct with explicit statements for base models.

claim: Prompt format injects non-evidential priors: option-label bias (gold to D lowers gpt-3.5-turbo from 67.2 to 60.9; to A lifts llama-30B 53.1 to 68.2) and example order (SST-2 54.3 to 93.4).
agent_test: Randomise option order and take the mean probability over permutations before normalising; compare to a single fixed order.
audit_note: Interpretive framing ('non-evidential priors'); Zhao's 54.3 to 93.4 is the SST-2 range across training-example permutations; Zheng's 67.2 to 60.9 and 53.1 to 68.2 match the abstract/Table 1.

claim: Aggregating sampled answers by vote or normalised probability beats single greedy CoT (GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2). On PaLM-540B, majority vote and length-normalised probability-weighted sum are within 0.3 points on all six tasks (e.g. GSM8K 74.4 vs 74.1); unnormalised weighting is worse (59.9). No equal-token test on 2025-26 models.
agent_test: Already verified against the paper; run equal-token comparison of N-sample vote vs one long chain.

claim: Verbalised confidence in RLHF models is better calibrated than token log-probabilities; large models are calibrated on multiple choice when the format is right; 'None of the above' hurts.
agent_test: Check calibration (ECE) of the verbalised distribution after code normalisation on a held-out set.
audit_note: Tian: verbalized confidence beats token probabilities for RLHF models; Kadavath: calibration on multiple choice depends on lettered-option format and 'none of the above' harms accuracy/calibration. Kadavath's models are pre-RLHF-era, so the two findings come from different model types.

claim: Without retrieval LLM forecasts are barely better than a coin flip (Brier .208 vs crowd .149, random .25); with retrieval and aggregation .179 vs .149.
agent_test: Brier-score the agent's normalised answer probabilities on held-out items.

claim: VERIFIED in the full paper (Mandel, Karvetski, Dhami 2018, N=50 UK analysts, one 4-hypothesis case). Forcing stated probabilities over exclusive hypotheses to sum to 1 cut mean absolute error from 0.23 to 0.15 (35%, d=0.96). Equal-weight averaging of all 50 coherentized judgments gave 0.09 (61%). Plain normalisation (divide by the sum) gave MAE 0.13, slightly better than the quadratic-programming method (0.15). Human analysts only: no LLM replication found.
agent_test: Log the sum of the model's raw option scores; compare raw vs normalised Brier at equal tokens. Expect gain only when the sum is far from 1.

claim: Whether GPT-3 shows the base-rate fallacy is contested: it answered the cab problem about right, but small changes (black cab, option order) flipped answers.
agent_test: Run base-rate items with adversarial rewordings; measure answer stability.

claim: Letting the LLM propose factors and coarse levels while code computes the probabilities (BIRD) beats LLM-only probability judgment in pairwise preference (F1 59 percent, over 30 percent above GPT-4).
agent_test: Same split on our tasks: model gives likelihood labels, code multiplies and normalises.

claim: Bayesian models of ICL (latent-concept inference, scaling laws) fit LLM behaviour but good fit does not prove a Bayesian mechanism.
agent_test: Descriptive; no direct test.
audit_note: Arora et al. state explicitly that non-Bayesian laws fit equally well so they do not claim LLMs are Bayesian; Xie et al. prove their result only in an HMM toy setting.

claim: Hard elimination from LLM 'ruled out' calls is risky: asking models to name the wrong option is less accurate than asking for the right one in every model and dataset tested (GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, Falcon; small models below 50/50), and over iterative elimination rounds raw accuracy falls (about .834 to .768 for LLaMA-2 70B, .526 to .232 for 7B on ARC; table read from layout). No study compares zero versus soft down-weighting directly.
agent_test: Run elimination with a probability floor (for example 0.02) and a revive rule against a hard zero; measure how often the gold answer is zeroed.

claim: The weak link in an LLM Bayes update is the verbalised likelihood, not the arithmetic. With GPT-5.1 and others, about half of batch-mode wrong-direction updates moved toward a better (GPT-5.1) likelihood than the model's own, and swapping in oracle likelihoods gave large gains where the model's own differed most. Word-valued premises were solved by GPT-4-Turbo in only 8.7% of QUITE cases.
agent_test: Elicit P(E|H) as numbers on a fixed scale, check them against a second sample, and test update accuracy using oracle versus own likelihoods.

claim: Offloading the arithmetic to code works when the quantities are given: GPT-4 with extract-then-ProbLog reached about 98% on Bayesian-network word problems versus roughly 29% for chain-of-thought; reasoning plus Python closed the gap on a no-closed-form posterior for Gemini-2.5-Pro (40 runs).
agent_test: Keep the model's job to extraction and likelihood judgment; let code compute and normalise.

claim: Option position and label bias is large and removable by permutation averaging in 2023 models (cyclic permutation at 4x cost: llama-2-70B accuracy 50.8 to 54.7; PriDe gets most of the gain at 1.15-3.4x), but no 2025-26 frontier-model measurement was found; 2025-26 papers test 3B-32B models only.
agent_test: Measure answer-position effect on the target frontier model by shuffling gold position; if over 2 points, average over cyclic orderings.

claim: Cross-conversation elicitation of exclusive-option probabilities often fails to sum to 1 (over 50% of 30 scenarios for almost all model-constraint pairs, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen-2.5-32B) but within one dialogue violations fall to about 10% (Gemini) or 1 of 30 (Gemma).
agent_test: Elicit all option scores in one call and normalise in code; do not elicit them in separate calls.

claim: Prior stated in the prompt: base models ignore a stated coin bias; instruction-tuned models (up to about 8B) follow it better but still start from a biased pretraining prior, and in-context evidence outweighs the stated bias. No frontier-model test found.
agent_test: Test whether a numeric prior supplied in the prompt shifts a frontier model's posterior as Bayes predicts; otherwise keep the prior in code.

claim: A frontier-model scaffold that keeps a probability-ranked differential with Bayesian updating after each finding (MAI-DxO with o3) scored 81.9% vs 78.6% for plain o3 on 304 NEJM cases, but the Bayesian role was not ablated, and probabilities were model-stated, not code-computed.
agent_test: Ablate the probability-ranked differential role in a similar scaffold before crediting it.

claim: No LLM study using Jeffrey conditionalization (uncertain evidence) was found in this gap search; the handling of uncertain evidence in a scaffold has no measured support. Gap 7 stays open.
agent_test: Compare hard conditioning with a likelihood-ratio update that uses the model's stated confidence in the evidence.
